claim: The industries provide significant economic stimulus by attracting visitation and tourism.

quotes: Melbourne's festivals, theatres and arts precincts drive tourism. In 2019 cultural visitors spent 2.5 times more than other tourists and live music alone contributes $1.7 billion to the state economy annually

Research shows public galleries are driving visitors to Melbourne and across the regions, with 49% of overnight trips to Melbourne and 44% of domestic trips to regional Victoria including a visit to a gallery by a growing cohort of high-spend arts tourists
more than 11 million Victorians and visitors came through the doors of our state-owned arts and cultural institutions in the last financial year alone
detail.critic_finding: Sources support the proposition for specific sub-sectors (performing arts, festivals, galleries) but the claim generalises to "the industries" without that qualification, making it broader than what any single passage asserts.
detail.source_says: Specific sub-sectors — including Melbourne's festivals, theatres, arts precincts, public galleries, and state-owned cultural institutions — are cited as drivers of tourism and visitation, with cultural visitors spending 2.5 times more than other tourists in 2019.
detail.so_what: The claim attributes tourism/visitation stimulus to "the industries" broadly; sources tie it specifically to performing arts, festivals, and public galleries — not all creative industries uniformly.

claim: Victoria rated higher for cultural participation than all other jurisdictions surveyed, including New York, Sweden and the UK.

quotes: Victoria rated higher for cultural participation than all other jurisdictions where this research has been undertaken. This includes New York City, Sweden and the UK.
detail.critic_finding: The source says Victoria rated higher than jurisdictions "where this research has been undertaken" and lists NYC, Sweden and the UK — not "all other jurisdictions surveyed." The summary substitutes "all other jurisdictions surveyed" for the source's narrower phrase, slightly overstating the scope of comparison. The summary also says "New York" where the source says "New York City."
detail.source_says: Victoria rated higher for cultural participation than all other jurisdictions where the Audience Atlas research has been undertaken, including New York City, Sweden and the UK.
detail.so_what: The source says "other jurisdictions where this research has been undertaken," not "all other jurisdictions surveyed globally"; the UK is mentioned, not "the UK" as a country-level comparator identical to the claim.

claim: Engagement with the industries brings communities together, breaks down barriers between groups, and encourages cohesion.

detail.so_what: Reader would believe a specific claim was made in testimony when no witness stated it in those terms.

claim: A growing body of evidence recognises the role arts and creativity play in positive mental health and wellbeing outcomes.

quotes: The research out of Western Australia – its catchphrase is 'You don't have to be good at the arts for the arts to be good for you.' They recommend 2 hours of any kind of art activity a week, and it can improve your mental health by 30 per cent.
Research from Western Australia suggests two-hours of art-making per week can improve mental health6, due to its emphasis on self-expression, creativity, enjoyment and social inclusion.
A growing body of research demonstrates that the arts can help address the pressing mental health and wellbeing challenges faced by many Victorians.
Participation in the arts is proven to improve mental health outcomes. Surveys show that over 70% of Melbourne Fringe participants report positive impacts on their mental wellbeing.
detail.critic_finding: The claim is well-supported across multiple written submissions but is not attributed to any specific witness's oral testimony; the closest oral evidence is Robertson (PGAV) citing Western Australian research. The claim is accurate but broader than any single sourced assertion.
detail.source_says: Multiple written submissions cite research showing arts participation can improve mental health outcomes, including a Western Australian study recommending 2 hours of art-making per week to improve mental health by 30%, and Melbourne Fringe data showing over 70% of participants report positive mental wellbeing impacts.
detail.so_what: Reader would think this is a direct witness assertion, but it appears only in written submissions, not as a witness's own oral testimony.

claim: COVID-19 severely damaged the industries, limiting opportunities to present/engage publicly and restricting practitioners' income.

The industry experienced a sharp decline in employment of 7% in the first year of the COVID-19 pandemic, and then recovered in the latter years of the pandemic. Despite this recovery, employment in the industry in 2022–23 was 1% lower compared to pre-COVID-19 levels in 2018–19, suggesting that the industry continues to experience some financial difficulties.
detail.critic_finding: Multiple passages confirm COVID-19 forced venue closures, restricted public engagement and presentations, and severely cut practitioner income — matching the claim's subject, scope, and direction without overstatement.

claim: COVID-19 took away critical training opportunities from those looking to enter the industries.

quotes: The decrease in possible 'gigs' has also impacted music students in Victoria, meaning they are less likely to find music work to sustain them during their studies. These financial impacts have affected the quality and quantity of the music graduate pipeline in Victoria

These measures disproportionately impacted the creative arts industry as galleries, museums, theatres, live venues, and pubs were forced to close their doors as restrictions impacted audience numbers and forced productions and exhibitions to cease or move elsewhere.
they led to a significant increase in anxiety and depression in young people and a number of skills are missing
detail.critic_finding: Sources describe COVID reducing gigs for music students, closing venues, and causing skill gaps — adjacent harms to training quality/volume, not a direct removal of training opportunities as the claim asserts.
detail.source_says: COVID-19 reduced performance opportunities for music students, caused skill gaps in young people, and disrupted arts industry activity, harming the pipeline of emerging creative workers — but sources do not state training opportunities were "taken away."
detail.so_what: Reader would think COVID eliminated training opportunities outright; sources describe degraded or reduced work/skills opportunities, not removal of training per se.

claim: Exclusion from COVID-19 financial support programs exacerbated financial issues and created ongoing skill gaps.

quotes: While the Australia Government introduced schemes such as JobKeeper to enable workers to retain an income, many creative workers were ineligible for the scheme because they could not demonstrate 12 months of continuous employment with one employer.

while targeted COVID-19 support was provided by Commonwealth and State Governments at the peak of the pandemic, national support was primarily through JobKeeper payments and the Boosting Cash Flow for Employers program, which most independent artists were ineligible to apply for.
Critical skills have been lost in the industry, particularly in production and technical areas.
The lack of technical people that can do technical work – they have left the industry because they were not supported.
detail.critic_finding: Sources confirm exclusion from COVID support exacerbated financial hardship, and separately that skill gaps emerged. But the claim that exclusion "created ongoing skill gaps" conflates two distinct causal chains not directly linked in the passages.
detail.source_says: Exclusion from COVID-19 financial support (e.g. JobKeeper) worsened financial hardship for creative workers; separately, skill gaps emerged as technical workers left the industry due to lack of support during the pandemic.
detail.so_what: Sources support exclusion worsening financial hardship and skill/workforce loss, but do not explicitly link exclusion itself as the cause of skill gaps — skill gaps are attributed to workers leaving the industry, not directly to exclusion from support programs.

claim: Children's and young people's creative participation and attendance declined significantly between 2017–18 and 2021–22.

quotes: Between 2017–18 and 2021–22 attendance at performing arts events by children dropped from 40% to 31%, and adult attendance at cultural venues fell from 86% to 69%.
detail.critic_finding: The source covers children's attendance at performing arts events (a specific subset) and adult cultural venue attendance — not "children's and young people's creative participation" as a broad category. The claim merges two distinct data points and expands scope beyond what the source says.
detail.source_says: Between 2017–18 and 2021–22, attendance at performing arts events by children dropped from 40% to 31%, and adult attendance at cultural venues fell from 86% to 69%.
detail.so_what: The reader would think children's creative participation broadly declined, but the source only shows children's performing arts attendance specifically, not creative participation generally.

claim: Several live music venues have closed following COVID-19 due to pressures such as rising costs and inconsistent financial support.

quotes: 1300 live music venues in Australia, including 256 in Victoria alone have closed since COVID-19 began (ref).

parts of the arts sector were not supported through COVID, so they have disappeared. The lack of technical people that can do technical work – they have left the industry because they were not supported.
We have had music venues citing increases of eight times, nine times what they were paying a few years ago, and it has got to the point where a lot of them just cannot operate.
detail.critic_finding: Sources confirm closures and rising costs, but the scale is 256 in Victoria / 1,300 nationally — not merely "several." "Inconsistent financial support" is also a partial characterisation of the causes cited (insurance spikes, licensing, COVID ineligibility, etc.).
detail.source_says: 1,300 live music venues across Australia, including 256 in Victoria, have closed since COVID-19 began, with insurance costs (rising 8–9 times), licensing fees, and lack of COVID support eligibility cited as key pressures.
detail.so_what: Reader would underestimate the scale: 256 Victoria / 1,300 Australia venues closed — far more than "several"; also the causes are broader than stated.

claim: It has never been harder for Victorians to make a living in the industries.

quotes: the Artists as Workers report has shown that it's never been harder for Australian artists to make a living — with only 9 per cent able to dedicate all their working time at their creative practice.
the 2024 Artists as Workers report from Creative Australia showed it's 'never been harder' for Australian artists to make a living.
detail.critic_finding: The source consistently attributes the "never been harder" finding to Australian artists broadly (from a national Creative Australia report), not specifically to Victorians.
detail.source_says: The 2024 Artists as Workers report (Creative Australia) found it has never been harder for Australian artists — not specifically Victorians — to make a living.
detail.so_what: Reader would think the claim is specifically about Victorians, but the source refers to Australian artists nationally.

claim: Insecure or low wages impact retention and discourage people from pursuing a career in the industries.

quotes: TNA's research found that in 2024, 59 per cent of independent artists had considered leaving the sector and 33 per cent had taken active steps to do so. Reasons for leaving include burnout, lack of employment opportunities and financial unsustainability.

A lot of stage managers and production managers went off and worked in other sideline industries or went off and worked in other operational roles. They love the arts and the creative industries, but actually they are making a judgement call for themselves. Is it worth what you said in terms of their mental health, their families and what support they need to provide, what money they can earn?

In TNA's 2024 Member Survey, 59% of independent artists said they have considered leaving the arts industry, with 33% saying they have taken action to leave the industry (such as retraining). The main reasons for considering leaving the industry were:
• Burnout (53%)
• Lack of employment/work (46%)
• Seeking better pay/benefits (43%) and seeking a better work/life balance (43%)

the Artists as Workers report has shown that it's never been harder for Australian artists to make a living — with only 9 per cent able to dedicate all their working time at their creative practice. Overall artist income barely exceeds minimum wage (falling 26 per cent below the national average and 45 per cent less than similarly-educated workers).
detail.critic_finding: Sources support financial precarity/low pay contributing to people leaving the sector, but the claim conflates retention with discouraging entry, and the sources cite burnout and lack of work as equally prominent reasons alongside pay.
detail.source_says: Low pay and financial unsustainability are among several reasons (alongside burnout, lack of work, and work-life balance) why existing arts workers consider or take steps to leave the sector; sources do not specifically address discouraging people from entering the industries.
detail.so_what: Reader may think wages alone drive attrition; sources show burnout, lack of work, and work-life balance are equal or larger drivers, and the evidence is mostly about retention, not entry into the industries.

claim: Many who want to engage with the industries cannot afford to due to the cost-of-living crisis.

the only way we can meet these increasing costs is obviously by increasing our ticket prices. That then, conversely, reduces our audience numbers due to the lack of affordability for them to attend our shows

claim: Victoria receives its fair share of funding from Creative Australia.

Creative Australia's 2023–24 annual report shows that Victoria received $28.7 million, or 27 per cent, of the investment that it made, which is a significant uplift from the previous year of $18.9 million. That is sitting against 26 per cent of the national population in Victoria at that particular time, so on a per capita basis it is relatively close.

This data indicates that on average over the last decade, against population, Victoria has received a proportionally larger share of national arts and cultural spending from Creative Australia (+2.9%), second only to the Northern Territory.
on average the Vic population over the last decade has been 25.7 per cent of the Australian population and has received 28.6 per cent of the funding, so that is 2.9 per cent higher.
